schema_ddl:
CREATE TABLE EMPLOYEE (
    EMPID INT,
    NAME VARCHAR(255),
    SUPERVISOR INT,
    SALARY INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (EMPID),
    CHECK (EMPID <> SUPERVISOR),
    CHECK (SALARY >= 0)
);

CREATE TABLE BONUS (
    EMPID INT,
    BONUS INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (EMPID),
    FOREIGN KEY (EMPID) REFERENCES EMPLOYEE(EMPID),
    CHECK (BONUS >= 0)
);
q1: SELECT EMPLOYEE.NAME, BONUS.BONUS FROM EMPLOYEE LEFT JOIN BONUS ON EMPLOYEE.EMPID = BONUS.EMPID WHERE BONUS < 1000 OR BONUS IS NULL
q2: SELECT NAME, BONUS FROM (SELECT NAME, BONUS FROM EMPLOYEE E LEFT JOIN BONUS B ON E.EMPID=B.EMPID) A WHERE BONUS<1000 OR BONUS IS NULL
q1_prompt_sql: SELECT EMPLOYEE.NAME, BONUS.BONUS FROM EMPLOYEE LEFT JOIN BONUS ON EMPLOYEE.EMPID = BONUS.EMPID WHERE BONUS < 1000 OR BONUS IS NULL
q2_prompt_sql: SELECT NAME, BONUS FROM (SELECT NAME, BONUS FROM EMPLOYEE E LEFT JOIN BONUS B ON E.EMPID=B.EMPID) A WHERE BONUS<1000 OR BONUS IS NULL
counterexample: INSERT INTO EMPLOYEE (EMPID, NAME, SUPERVISOR, SALARY) VALUES (1, 'Employee1', 2, 5000); INSERT INTO BONUS (EMPID, BONUS) VALUES (1, NULL);
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are not semantically equivalent because of the placement of the WHERE clause. In Q1, the WHERE clause is applied after the LEFT JOIN, which can lead to rows being filtered out that should not be, especially when the BONUS is NULL. In Q2, the WHERE clause is applied after the subquery, which correctly preserves all rows from the EMPLOYEE table, including those with NULL BONUS values.
counterexample_dsp: The test data should include an employee with a NULL BONUS value. In Q1, this employee will be filtered out, while in Q2, they will be included in the result set.
